newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans reach historic budget, tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans reach historic budget, tax deal.

text.p: After months of hard-fought negotiations, President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders on Monday reached an accord to balance the federal budget for the first time in a generation and cut taxes by $90 billion over the next five years.

The historic agreement worked out by a Democratic president and leaders of the majority Republicans in Congress will also boost spending on education by $40 billion and start a $24 billion health insurance programme for uninsured children.

White House aides said the president was very pleased nad many of his congressional Democrats, who were generally left out of the talks, said they liked what they had seen of it. House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri reserved judgment.

"This is an historic opportunity. It can be the achievement of a generation," the president told governors meeting in Las Vegas. Clinton was wrapping up a three-day trip to the western United States while the budget and tax package was being wrapped up in Washington.

White House spokesman Joe Lockhart said Clinton would have more to say about it on Tuesday. "The president was pleased with the information and was looking forward to a full briefing in the morning," he said.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici beamed as they announced the deal at a hastily assembled news conference in the Senate.

The Republicans stressed that all sides made gains in the negotiations. "We want this to be viewed as a win-win situation. We gave ground and the administration gave ground and we found common ground," Lott of Mississippi said.

"When you add the package up, it is a splendid one for all Americans and we are very proud to be part of it. Hopefully, the president feels the same way and many Democrats, so that we will get bipartisan support," Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, added.
The White House aides who negotiated with Congress were clearly pleased with their work.

"It's a good balanced budget agreement and it does the kinds of things that need to be done for the country," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters. Clinton's Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles said he will report to the president: "We could not be more pleased with the outcome."

Although they said the deal was "tentative," all that remained was to write the legislation which will be brought before the House and Senate for votes this week. Lawmakers were optimistic on its chances for passage.
Clinton sought and received assurances that three issues had been taken care of: spending for education, a child tax credit, and an expansion of health benefits for poor children.

Republicans also won provisions including a cut in the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent, down from the current 28 percent, and a second drop to 18 percent in 2001 for long-term holdings. Estate taxes were also eased.

The $500-per-child tax credit was extended as Clinton wanted to those who earn as little as $18,000 a year and boosted on the other side to cover most of the middle class with a phase-out starting at $110,000 as Republicans sought. This tax credit will be worth $85 billion over five years.

To bring the budget to balance, the plan slows the rate of growth in many federal social programmes and reduces Medicare costs by $115 billion over five years. At the last minute lawmakers and the White House backed off a plan to require wealthier senior citizens to pay higher Medicare premiums.
But Republicans won acceptance of a new Medicare medical savings-account pilot programme that allows 390,000 seniors to open the tax-free accounts as an alternative to Medicare.
The plan will raise the 24 cent-per-pack cigarette tax by 15 cents and will extend the airline ticket tax to raise about $30 billion through 2002.

Clinton won a new $24 billion programme to provide health insurance to cover up to 2.2 million uninsured children. They also accepted his education proposals including $31 billion in Hope scholarships for post-secondary studies.

These last items convinced one of the Republicans' harshest critics, Democratic Whip David Bonior of Michigan, that he liked the plan. "All and all when you look at the distribution here I think working families did quite well on eudcation and child tax credits and that's really the key part of the tax proposal."

Another veteran Democrat, Representative David Obey of Wisconsin, who has fought Republicans to retain federal programmes for families and education, left the briefing by admininstration officials in a huff, remarking: "I've heard enough." Gephardt said only, "We haven't had a chance to understand it or analyse it."
